history.content: I want to know whether my building is big enough.

Give me two things: the inside measurements, and the ages of the birds you want to put in it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so I also need to know which of the two you are building.
Seven metres by four, the commercial model, and I want breeders and growers both.

draws.answer: Then you are on the right mix, because the reference keeps seven by four for breeders and nine by three for the growers, and seven per square metre suits both at 8 by 4 metres and at 5 by 5. But the reference does not say how many of each you need, so I will not give a count for yours. What it does say is what each group needs: at least two weather-protected shelters, one for the breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre and one for the growers at 12 to 15, well away from the henhouse, and a grassy run for the adults, a manure pit, and the droppings pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep. Check that at your own dimensions. For the chick room the same goes, one room, 50 birds at 50 per square metre, and two sitters, 7.5 by 5. Keep the ground clear of the litter in both cases, because a muddy floor is what keeps birds from changing it. The brooder is the one where the chicks go the first three weeks. Ask ICAT what is available near you.

Then you are outside what the commercial model is built on, and that is the reason to plan the size properly. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for growers, so seven by four is 28 square metres, which gives you roughly 1,400 birds at 60 eggs per hen and 21.6 chicks. The 2017 ESFT compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so the same size is well below it and you would be doubling the number of birds, which is a different farm. Either way, the two figures are different. Set the same building inside either 28 square metres, which would mean you would need about 1,200 eggs at 60 to 65, or a grid of 12 to 15 by 10, which would mean about 1,800 chicks and 66 to 75 eggs. Take both to ICAT before you spend anything.

draws.answer: Not two months. The six production cycles of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference are 25 to 30 days for the eggs, 30 to 35 for the chicks and 55 to 60 for the growers, and the whole unit runs on six production cycles a year, not on a bird moving from one sale to the next. The birds spend two months at the brooder, then three weeks in the chick room, then three weeks in the grower compartment, at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, before the chick room is moved out and the grower compartment is filled. The six cycles is the time you expect to be in the chick room, not the route the birds take.

In that reference the birds are sold as birds, not as birds from eggs. In your case the figures are the same, so the timing is closer and the result is the same, but the reference is a method, not a plan: the money comes from the selling of the birds, not from the hatching.

per_item.reference: Look under the leaves of your tomato plants every week to detect any tiny insects. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide on any spray. If the insects are numerous, prune the most infested leaves and destroy them. Remove weeds from the plot edges that can serve as a refuge for the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong water jet to wash off aphids, while ladybirds and lacewings will naturally suppress them. For the approved product and dosage, contact ICAT.

history.content: The leaves on my tomatoes are yellowing and I hear a faint buzzing, what's the first thing I should do?

draws.answer: Those signs point to whiteflies or aphids attacking your tomato crop. Begin by shaking the plant and inspecting the leaf undersides for the tiny insects. Next, turn the leaves over and count the pests on a few plants to decide if treatment is necessary. Then remove the most infested leaves and destroy them, and clear weeds that may harbor the pests around the field. Deploy yellow sticky traps for whiteflies, and apply a strong jet of water along with ladybirds or lacewings for aphids. When the infestation is heavy, seek advice from ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

The first thing is to check the underside of the leaves for the presence of whiteflies and aphids, because the two pests need different control. Turn the tomato leaves over and count the insects on several plants; low numbers may mean no treatment is needed. Next, shake each plant and look before you spray, as using the wrong name wastes spray and money. Remove the most heavily infested leaves, destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. For the approved spray and its rate, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.

draws.answer: Year 1: legumes, year 2: maize. The figure I do have is one region's and I will not supply it anywhere else: in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize goes with a cereal with the legume, maize with cowpea or with cassava and maize together, and in Centrale, Kara and Savanes maize goes with sorghum, millet or with beans. Year 3: a root or tuber crop, year 4: an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, yam. In the south the brochure's rule carries a maize first, then a legume, year by year.

Year 1, the improving plants: legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen, soya or cowpea. Year 2, an intermediate that takes the nitrogen left by the legumes, such as maize, millet or sorghum. Year 3, a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam, sweetpotato or yangon. Year 4, the fallow. The four year example the catalogue gives is maize, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow.

history.content: How should I transplant and fertilise my rice seedlings?

draws.answer: Transplant seedlings after about 21 days in the nursery. First raise seedlings for roughly 21 days in the nursery then transplant them 20 by 20 centimetres. Then, at 10-15 days after transplant, spread 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 about a hundred and fifty days after transplanting. Apply 100 kilograms per hectare of urea, which is the same amount as the 200 kg, in a pocket-widths five hundredth of a hectare after transplant. Finally, apply 50 kilograms per hectare of phosphate at panicle initiation, using two bags for a quarter-hectare field. Weed the field at 15-25 days after transplant and again around 40 days, then protect against birds from flowering until harvest. For any variety or rate adjustment, consult ICAT.

draws.answer: Then the compartment is the problem, not the number of hens: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on six production cycles a year, about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, all at one hen per square metre for the breeder compartment. That is the trouble the model is built to handle, and the figure gives you exactly what it is. It says a henhouse is a unit where disease comes from one place: the germs that travel in the droppings and secretions of the animals living or coming in, and where they stay. So empty on one end is the sign to look for at a flock that has spread. Check the water first, because a shortage of drinkers and siphon handles a crowding without one: the rule is water freely available, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. Then look at the feeder and the drinker, which should be enough for the age, and check whether the chicks have their own, apart feeders. If the crowd comes from people, look at the visitors.

Continue with the second weeding and earthing-up as scheduled. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, you should see ICAT.

draws.answer: The pale lower leaves of your maize after heavy rain are typical of nitrogen loss. Open a shallow drainage channel to let excess water run off the field. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, applying about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation and keep the fertilizer off the plant to avoid burn damage. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you later see streaks or dead-hearts, consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is bloat affecting your nanny goat. Immediately get the goat on its feet and keep it moving, holding its head raised to help belching. After that, drench a little vegetable or mineral oil into its mouth to break the froth and free the gas. This helps the rumen work again and lets the gas escape. The condition can lead to collapse very quickly. Call the veterinary service immediately for emergency assistance.

per_item.reference: Your cattle have gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Call the veterinary service the same day because only they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet that the urine is yellow-brown without red, which points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animal in the shade, give it clean water within reach, and do not make it walk because it lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you can see on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to stop further spread. See the veterinary service the same day.

Are the gums and eyelids pale or white?

draws.answer: Your cattle likely have gall sickness caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, as yellow-brown urine points to gall sickness. Keep the sick animals in the shade with clean water nearby and avoid making them walk because they are low on red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick animal, to prevent further spread. Never use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness spreads on contaminated needles. See the veterinary service the same day.

per_item.reference: Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.

history.content: I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

draws.answer: The guidance I can give is to keep a part of any surplus good for sale at the time, not to sell it immediately. You should weigh the cost of storage against the potential price gain, because storing the beans lets you sell them dearer later. First, sort the beans and, if you can, dry them well so they are snappy and the moisture content is about 13-14%, which stops mold from developing. Then clean the store and take away all last-season residues where the larger grain borer might carry over. After that, place the dried beans in sound, sealed bags or bins and mix an approved storage insecticide such as an Actellic type at the labelled dose. If you still find insects, contact ICAT for the currently approved storage product.

Selling your bean bag at harvest is the common practice in Togo, and the study puts it as a good time to sell, about six months after harvest, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, so it is near the record price. But first check the market: if the price is low, the bag may be lost. Then treat the beans as an undemanding storage leg, which is drying them out so they hold, and keep them after the sale. For the best current outlet, ask a cooperative or ICAT, and ask ICAT for this season's outlet.
